name: Andropogon

project_scope.note: Older Texas source names remain searchable. Andropogon gerardii maps to canonical Andropogon gerardi; A. glomeratus maps to canonical Anatherum glomeratum; A. virginicus maps to reviewed Anatherum virginicum range HOLD.

study_strategy.warning: Do not identify these grasses from fall color alone. The inflorescence architecture is the fastest reliable split.

quick_split: Andropogon gerardi — accepted Kew name, alias A. gerardii; several stout exposed terminal racemes, often turkey-foot; old physical photo gallery roles corrected 2026-10-21.
Anatherum glomeratum — dense broomlike silky cluster near the top; formerly Andropogon glomeratus.
Anatherum virginicum — slender silky racemes partly enclosed by spathe-like sheaths; formerly Andropogon virginicus, held in this project's existing review.
Schizachyrium scoparium — many separate SHORT hairy racemes on different upper leafy branches.
Bothriochloa ischaemum (KR) — several narrower, longer terminal fingers can superficially resemble turkey-foot; verify leaf collar and paired spikelets.
comparison_lesson.caveat: Older Texas floras place all three familiar plants in Andropogon; the learner keeps those aliases searchable while displaying the current accepted Kew names.

visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — genus now has seven source-credited photo panels and eleven reused visible-anatomy arrows; true full turkey-foot base and Hays ordinary bushy head missing

source_concept_status.learner_action: comparison-only; no canonical install while Anatherum virginicum remains range HOLD

look_here_first: BIG BLUESTEM (current ANDROPOGON GERARDI): start at the ENTIRE TOP OF A FLOWERING CULM and trace where 2–6 relatively STOUT exposed spikelet-bearing RACEMES originate close together, commonly forming a 3-pronged turkey-foot. Then check one paired sessile/pedicelled spikelet and bent awn, plus actual collar morphology. DO NOT label the existing collar-only macro as a whole plant, and DO NOT call a tight close crop of three racemes a verified shared-base turkey-foot silhouette. Little bluestem has MANY SHORT silky racemes on separate leafy upper branches; bushy bluestem (NOW ANATHERUM GLOMERATUM) has a compact BRUSH of partly sheathed silky racemes; KR bluestem is introduced and typically presents several longer, thinner terminal fingers; Indiangrass has ONE golden BRANCHED panicle with its characteristic rifle-sight collar. Preserve accepted genus taxonomy and all science/range holds.
photo_truth_guardrail: Old Andropogon gerardi image file names are not anatomical evidence. New visual arrows point only to independently reviewed macro features; non-isolated mixed-grass photographs remain unarrowed.

visual_comparison.title: Andropogon — big bluestem's stout racemes versus nearby grass look-alikes
visual_comparison.subtitle: Seven existing credited REAL source photographs, eleven inherited visible-organ arrows across three big bluestem, little bluestem and KR bluestem images. Genus scope distinguishes modern Andropogon gerardi from the old 'Andropogon glomeratus' = Anatherum glomeratum. No new rights, photo bytes or taxon certification.

items.label: 4 · LITTLE BLUESTEM COMPARISON — short silky racemes along leafy branches
items.image_role: Source-labelled Montana wild-type little bluestem, close-up of flowering branches bearing distinct short silky racemes and subtending sheaths

visual_comparison.memory_rule: BIG: FEW STOUT EXPOSED TURKEY-FOOT RACEMES. LITTLE: MANY SHORT SILKY BRANCH RACEMES. BUSHY: DENSE SOFT BRUSH. KR: MANY LONG THIN FINGERS. INDIAN: ONE GOLDEN BRANCHED PANICLE.

comparison_cards.title: Big bluestem vs Little bluestem — long finger vs short silky branches
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Trace the whole reproductive culm: BIG bluestem bears 2–6 long relatively stout, mostly EXPOSED racemes near the culm tip (often 'turkey foot'); LITTLE bluestem bears numerous much SHORTER white-silky racemes from separate upper leafy branches. The photos show individual real units; none alone can replace a complete top-of-stem photograph.

field_matrix.big: Few thick racemes converging at the top
field_matrix.little: Many short racemes scattered along branches

field_matrix.big: More exposed long raceme, hairy paired spikelets
field_matrix.little: Short silk-tipped raceme emerging from subtending sheath

field_matrix.big: Three verified original macro/collar photographs, 6 broad arrows
field_matrix.little: Existing source-photo short racemes with 3 arrows

comparison_cards.caution: Season, mowing and immature heads may prevent reliable identification; use sheath/ligule and mature seedhead.

comparison_cards.title: Big bluestem vs introduced KR bluestem
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both can show fingerlike terminal branches. Big bluestem's racemes are generally more stout (often just 2–6); KR bluestem often has more and thinner, longer fingers arising near the terminal head. Confirm spikelet details and basal leaf collar rather than relying on finger count alone.

field_matrix.big: Strong ONLY if mature attached head and collar match

comparison_cards.caution: Do not call KR bluestem native or identify either from vegetative leaf color.

comparison_cards.title: Big bluestem vs bushy bluestem (now Anatherum glomeratum)
comparison_cards.look_here_first: BIG = discrete OPEN exposed 2–6 stout racemes. BUSHY = clustered, crowded silky short racemes partly enclosed by spathe-like sheaths, giving a cottony BRUSH top. Older field guides list Bushy as Andropogon glomeratus; it is a cross-genus LOOK-ALIKE in this current learner.

field_matrix.big: True body parts pictured but no entire local turkey-foot photographed
field_matrix.bushy: Existing Midway Atoll var. pumilus photo is not verified Texas diagnostic; local exact ordinary-form macro still needed

comparison_cards.caution: Source-labelled Hawai‘i var. pumilus is NOT a certified representative of the local Texas variety. Do not create extra Andropogon species.

comparison_cards.title: Big bluestem vs Indiangrass — turkey foot vs one golden plume
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Big bluestem has a few stout terminal RACEMES like turkey toes. Indiangrass has one internally BRANCHED elongated golden panicle and a conspicuous tall pointed membranous 'rifle sight' leaf ligule; their paired spikelet anatomy also differs.

field_matrix.big: Hair fringe and relatively short membrane
field_matrix.indiangrass: Conspicuous raised membrane with pointed corners

field_matrix.big: Developed pedicelled and fertile sessile paired units
field_matrix.indiangrass: Fertile sessile unit + naked sterile pedicel

comparison_cards.caution: A single golden color or tall bunch is not a reliable separator; photograph full panicle and opened collar.
